title: Corvus. Coronis. Cornix. Ocyroe
titleEn: The Raven, Coronis, and Ocyrhoe — Metamorphoses II.531–675
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Juno takes to the air behind peacocks newly painted since Argus was killed, and Ovid turns aside to a second bird whose colour changed: the raven, white once, now on his way to tell Apollo that Coronis has been unfaithful. A crow overtakes him with a long warning drawn from her own life — she too reported what she had seen to a goddess, and she too was demoted for it — but the raven flies on and tells. Watch how much of this part is birds arguing about whether truth-telling pays, and how the colour white keeps turning: the raven's feathers, Coronis' limbs under her own blood. It ends in Chiron's cave, where the rescued child is being raised and the centaur's daughter sings a prophecy she is not allowed to finish.

advisory.lede: The crow's story turns on an attempted rape: a sea-god pursues her along the shore, and she escapes only by being turned into a bird. The same speech accuses Nyctimene of defiling her father's bed.
advisory.more: Ovid gives the pursuit itself half a line — the god readies force and follows — and then several lines to the girl's flight, her exhaustion in the soft sand, and her cry to gods and men that no mortal answers. Her rescue is a transformation, not a deliverance: she loses her arms, her clothing, her breast and her human feet, and the poem calls that help. The incest on Lesbos is named in a single clause, and the crow lays the blame on the daughter rather than the father. Both passages are presented here unaltered and translated at the register the Latin sets.

sentences.t:
Di maris adnuerant: habili Saturnia curru
ingreditur liquidum pavonibus aethera pictis,
sentences.l: The gods of the sea had nodded assent: in her nimble chariot Saturnia enters the liquid upper air, drawn by painted peacocks,
sentences.i: The sea-gods had given their nod, and Saturnia rides up into the clear high air in her light chariot, behind her painted peacocks,
sentences.n: Saturnia is Juno, named from her father Saturn rather than by her own name — Ovid almost never calls her Juno in narrative. The peacocks are in the ablative because they draw the chariot. Note also that aethera keeps its Greek accusative ending, one of many Greek forms in this part, and that the pluperfect adnuerant hands over at once to the present ingreditur — the tense-shift is how Ovid speeds up.

sentences.t:
tam nuper pictis caeso pavonibus Argo,
quam tu nuper eras, cum candidus ante fuisses,
corve loquax, subito nigrantes versus in alas.
sentences.l: peacocks painted as lately, with Argus slain, as you lately were, though before you had been white, chattering raven, suddenly turned into blackening wings.
sentences.i: peacocks painted no longer ago — Argus once killed — than you yourself were, chattering raven: white before, and all at once turned into black wings.
sentences.n: Ovid breaks off to address one of his own characters directly — apostrophe, and he does it constantly; you will meet Apollo addressed the same way in a few lines. Caeso Argo is an ablative absolute, a self-contained 'with Argus slain' where English wants a clause; the line assumes you know that the hundred-eyed watchman's death is what gave the peacock its tail. Versus in alas is a plain passive, 'turned into wings', with the agent left unnamed here — the close of this part supplies him.

sentences.t:
Nam fuit haec quondam niveis argentea pennis
ales ut aequaret totas sine labe columbas
nec servaturis vigili Capitolia voce
cederet anseribus nec amanti flumina cycno.
sentences.l: For this bird was once silvery with snow-white feathers, so that she matched doves wholly without a blemish, and yielded neither to the geese that would one day save the Capitol with their wakeful cry, nor to the swan that loves the rivers.
sentences.i: For she was once a silver bird, snow-feathered, a match for the most spotless doves, and gave place neither to the geese who would one day save the Capitol with their watchful cry, nor to the river-loving swan.
sentences.n: Ales is feminine, so the raven is 'she' for as long as the bird is being described rather than addressed. Ut aequaret … cederet is a result clause: so white that she matched them. Servaturis is a future participle — geese 'destined to save' the Capitol, a Roman fact dropped centuries out of order into a Greek myth, which is exactly the sort of anachronism Ovid enjoys.

sentences.t:
Lingua fuit damno; lingua faciente loquaci
qui color albus erat, nunc est contrarius albo.
sentences.l: His tongue was his ruin; his chattering tongue doing the work, the colour that was white is now the opposite of white.
sentences.i: His tongue was his undoing; his chattering tongue did it, and the colour that was white is now white's opposite.
sentences.n: Lingua fuit damno uses the predicative dative — 'the tongue was for a harm', a construction Latin prefers to 'was a harm'. Lingua faciente loquaci is another ablative absolute. And Ovid will not write the word black: 'the opposite of white' is a joke at the raven's expense, and the whole tale exists to explain that one colour.

sentences.t:
Pulchrior in tota, quam Larisaea Coronis,
non fuit Haemonia: placuit tibi, Delphice, certe,
dum vel casta fuit vel inobservata.
sentences.l: None was more beautiful in all Haemonia than Larisaean Coronis: she pleased you, Delphic god, certainly — as long as she was either chaste or unwatched.
sentences.i: In all Haemonia there was no lovelier girl than Coronis of Larisa: she pleased you well enough, god of Delphi — so long as she was chaste, or at least unobserved.
sentences.n: Haemonia is Thessaly and Larisa one of its cities; the Delphic god is Apollo, addressed directly again. The last five words are the joke of the passage and it is a cold one: vel … vel offers the two conditions as equally good, so the god's love turns out to depend not on her fidelity but on his ignorance of it. Do not read it solemnly.

sentences.t:
Sed ales
sensit adulterium Phoebeius, utque latentem
detegeret culpam, non exorabilis index,
ad dominum tendebat iter.
sentences.l: But the bird of Phoebus sensed the adultery, and, so as to uncover the hidden fault — an informer no pleading could turn — he was bending his course toward his master.
sentences.i: But Phoebus' bird caught the adultery, and, an informer no pleading could turn, was making straight for his master to lay the hidden guilt bare.
sentences.n: Adulterium is the bird's framing, not a neutral fact: Coronis is nobody's wife, and the word imports a husband's grievance where there is none. Non exorabilis index stands in apposition, dropped in mid-sentence like an aside; exorabilis is what you are if entreaty can move you. Tendere iter is a set phrase, 'to direct one's road', and the imperfect leaves him still on the way, which is what lets the crow catch him.

sentences.t:
Quem garrula motis
consequitur pennis, scitetur ut omnia, cornix,
auditaque viae causa “non utile carpis”
inquit “iter:
sentences.l: And him the chattering crow follows on beating wings, to find out everything; and the reason for his journey having been heard, 'You are taking,' she says, 'a road that will do you no good:'
sentences.i: And the chattering crow comes after him on beating wings, to get the whole story out of him; and when she has heard where he is going, 'That road,' she says, 'will do you no good:'
sentences.n: Quem opening the sentence is the connecting relative — Latin's way of saying 'and him', not asking a question. Scitetur ut omnia is a purpose clause with a deponent verb, and audita viae causa yet another ablative absolute. The speech-tag inquit drops in between the adjective and its noun, so 'unprofitable' stands at the end of one line and 'road' at the head of the next.

sentences.t:
ne sperne meae praesagia linguae.
Quid fuerim quid simque vide, meritumque require:
sentences.l: do not scorn the forebodings of my tongue. See what I was and what I am, and ask what I earned by it:
sentences.i: do not make light of what my tongue foretells. Look at what I was and what I am, and ask what I got for it:
sentences.n: Ne sperne, a bare negative with the imperative, is verse's way of forbidding; prose would say noli spernere. Quid fuerim and quid simque are indirect questions and so take the subjunctive. Meritum is what one has deserved, and she means it bitterly — the reward turns out to be a demotion.

sentences.t:
invenies nocuisse fidem. Nam tempore quodam
Pallas Erichthonium, prolem sine matre creatam,
clauserat Actaeo texta de vimine cista
sentences.l: you will find that honesty did the harm. For once upon a time Pallas had shut Erichthonius — a child begotten without a mother — in a basket woven of Attic withies
sentences.i: you will find it was honesty that did the damage. For once Pallas shut Erichthonius — a child got without any mother — in a basket woven of Attic willow
sentences.n: Nocuisse fidem is an accusative and infinitive after invenies: 'that good faith did harm'. Fides here is the loyal reporting of what one has seen, and the whole part is an argument about whether it pays. Actaeus means Attic, from Acte, an old name for the region round Athens; the Latin says only that the child had no mother and leaves the rest to the reader.

sentences.t:
virginibusque tribus gemino de Cecrope natis
et legem dederat, sua ne secreta viderent.
sentences.l: and had given him to three maidens born of double-formed Cecrops, and had laid down a law: that they were not to look on her secrets.
sentences.i: and gave him to the three daughters of two-formed Cecrops, laying down a law with him: they were not to look at what she kept hidden.
sentences.n: One verb, dederat, has to serve both the girls and the law — Latin compresses where English would repeat. Geminus of Cecrops means half man and half serpent; the same adjective returns of Chiron at the end of this part, and both times it does the work of a whole sentence. Ne … viderent is the negative of an indirect command.

sentences.l: Hidden by the light leafage, I was watching from a thick elm what they would do. Two keep the trust without treachery, Pandrosos and Herse;
sentences.i: Hidden in the light leaves, I watched from a thick elm to see what they would do. Two of them kept the trust honestly, Pandrosos and Herse;
sentences.n: Abdita is feminine because the crow is feminine — and she was already a bird when she watched from the elm; her own transformation is told only afterwards, at 569, so the two halves of her speech run in reverse order of time. Quid facerent is an indirect question, and commissa is a participle used as a noun, 'the things entrusted', a common Latin economy. The shift from the imperfect speculabar to the present tuentur is the historic present taking over, exactly where the action is about to happen.

sentences.t:
timidas vocat una sorores
Aglauros nodosque manu diducit, et intus
infantemque vident adporrectumque draconem.
sentences.l: one calls her frightened sisters — Aglauros — and with her hand draws the knots apart, and inside they see both the baby and a serpent stretched out beside him.
sentences.i: one of them called her frightened sisters over — Aglauros — and pulled the knots apart with her hand, and inside they saw the baby, and a serpent stretched out beside him.
sentences.n: Una comes at the end of one line and the name Aglauros at the start of the next, so the culprit is identified a beat late: a favourite Ovidian suspension. The paired -que … -que means 'both … and'. Adporrectum keeps the edition's spelling with adp-, and means stretched out alongside — the snake is lying with the child, not coiled to strike.

sentences.t:
Acta deae refero. Pro quo mihi gratia talis
redditur, ut dicar tutela pulsa Minervae
et ponar post noctis avem.
sentences.l: I report the deed to the goddess. For which such gratitude is repaid to me, that I am declared driven out from Minerva's protection and am set below the bird of night.
sentences.i: I reported the deed to the goddess — and such is the gratitude repaid me: to be pronounced an outcast from Minerva's guardianship, and ranked below the bird of night.
sentences.n: Pulsa is nominative, agreeing with the speaker, and tutela is an ablative of separation: driven out from her protection. Gratia talis … ut is heavy irony — 'such thanks that …'. The bird of night is the owl, and the crow will not yet say the name; she holds Nyctimene back to the very end of her speech, where she can spit it.

sentences.t:
Mea poena volucres
admonuisse potest ne voce pericula quaerant.
sentences.l: My punishment can serve to have warned birds not to court dangers with their voice.
sentences.i: My punishment is warning enough to birds not to court danger with their voices.
sentences.n: Potest with a perfect infinitive, admonuisse, is a poetic idiom that comes out in English as a plain present — 'may warn'. Ne … quaerant is a negative purpose clause. Voce means specifically the speaking voice, which is the crow's whole subject: everything that goes wrong in this part goes wrong through somebody's tongue.

sentences.t:
At, puto, non ultro nec quicquam tale rogantem
me petiit? ipsa licet hoc a Pallade quaeras:
quamvis irata est, non hoc irata negabit.
sentences.l: But — I suppose — she did not come after me unasked, and me requesting nothing of the sort? You may ask this of Pallas herself: angry as she is, angry she will not deny this.
sentences.i: But I suppose she never sought me out of her own accord, when I had asked for nothing of the kind? You may put the question to Pallas herself: angry as she is, even angry she will not deny it.
sentences.n: Puto dropped in as a parenthesis is sarcasm — 'oh, I imagine …' — and the question expects the opposite answer to the one it pretends to want: of course the goddess came after her. Licet with the subjunctive quaeras gives 'you are free to ask'. Magnus prints nec quicquam, 'nor anything of the sort'; other editions print nequiquam, 'in vain', which turns the boast into a different one.

sentences.t:
Nam me Phocaica clarus tellure Coroneus
(nota loquor) genuit fueramque ego regia virgo
divitibusque procis (ne me contemne) petebar.
sentences.l: For Coroneus, famous in the Phocian land, begot me — I tell what is known — and I had been a royal maiden, and by wealthy suitors — do not despise me — I was sought.
sentences.i: For my father was Coroneus, a great man in the land of Phocis — this is common knowledge — and I was a king's daughter, courted by rich suitors: do not look down on me.
sentences.n: Two parentheses in three lines, and both are the crow interrupting herself to defend her own standing: she is wheedling. Fueram is a pluperfect where English is content with a simple past. Petebar, 'I was sought', is the same verb she used two lines earlier of Pallas coming after her, me petiit — in this speech even courtship is a pursuit.

sentences.l: My beauty was my ruin. For when along the shore, with slow steps, as I am used to do, I was strolling on the top of the sand, the god of the sea saw me and took fire;
sentences.i: My beauty was my ruin. One day, as I was strolling along the shore at my slow pace over the top of the sand, the way I like to, the sea-god saw me and took fire;
sentences.n: Forma nocuit answers nocuisse fidem a few lines above: first honesty harmed her, now beauty, and the crow's whole life is a list of things that turned out to be liabilities. Summa harena means the surface of the sand, the summus idiom that Latin uses where English says 'the top of'. Soleo stays present inside a past narrative — she still walks that way. Incaluit, 'grew hot', is the word Ovid keeps for the first stab of desire.

sentences.t:
utque precando
tempora cum blandis absumpsit inania verbis,
vim parat et sequitur.
sentences.l: and when by pleading he had spent his empty hours with coaxing words, he readies force and gives chase.
sentences.i: and when he had used up his time to no purpose, pleading and coaxing, he turned to force and came after me.
sentences.n: Tempora inania is proleptic: the hours are called empty because of how they turned out, not how they felt. Vim parat is the whole of Ovid's account of what the god decided to do, and vis in this context is sexual violence — two words, and then straight into the chase. The perfect absumpsit gives way to the presents parat and sequitur, and the pace changes with the tense.

sentences.t:
Fugio densumque relinquo
litus et in molli nequiquam lassor harena.
sentences.l: I flee, and I leave the hard-packed shore and am worn out to no purpose in the soft sand.
sentences.n: The two kinds of sand are the point: the densum litus is the firm wet strand where running works, the mollis harena the dry drift where it does not, and she has run from one into the other. Lassor is passive in form but middle in force, 'I grow weary'. The whole flight is told in the present tense, as if it were happening while she speaks.

sentences.t:
Inde deos hominesque voco; nec contigit ullum
vox mea mortalem: mota est pro virgine virgo
auxiliumque tulit.
sentences.l: Then I call gods and men; and my voice touched no mortal: a maiden was moved for a maiden, and brought help.
sentences.i: Then I called on gods and men, and my voice reached no mortal: it was a virgin who was moved for a virgin, and brought help.
sentences.n: Contingo with the accusative means to reach or touch, here of a cry reaching someone. Pro virgine virgo is the line's whole rhetoric: the two words are set side by side, one the goddess and one the girl, and the name Minerva is withheld — you are meant to work out which is which from the case endings alone.

sentences.t:
Tendebam bracchia caelo:
bracchia coeperunt levibus nigrescere pennis.
sentences.l: I was stretching my arms to heaven: my arms began to grow black with light feathers.
sentences.n: Caelo is a bare dative of direction, a poetic economy for ad caelum. The repetition of bracchia at the head of both halves is the technique of the whole transformation: the same word twice, and between the two it stops meaning the same thing. Four sentences in a row are built this way — arms, clothing, breast, feet.

sentences.t:
Reicere ex umeris vestem molibar: at illa
pluma erat inque cutem radices egerat imas.
sentences.l: I was struggling to throw my garment back off my shoulders: but it was plumage, and had driven roots deep into my skin.
sentences.i: I strove to throw the dress back off my shoulders: but it had become plumage, and had driven its roots deep into my skin.
sentences.n: Moliri is to labour at something that resists — the verb tells you the dress will not come. Radices egerat is a plant's metaphor, 'had driven roots down', so that for a moment the feathers are growing in her like a tree in soil. Imas, 'deepest', is thrown to the end of the line, which is where the horror of it lands.

sentences.t:
Plangere nuda meis conabar pectora palmis:
sed neque iam palmas nec pectora nuda gerebam.
sentences.l: I was trying to beat my bare breast with my palms: but I no longer had either palms or a bare breast.
sentences.n: Plangere pectora is the formal gesture of grief, the ritual beating of the breast — she reaches for the one action left to her and it too is gone. The nouns come back in the next line reversed, nuda … pectora … palmis becoming palmas … pectora nuda, and the palms change case as they go: an ablative of instrument in the first line, an accusative of what she no longer has in the second. Gerebam, 'I was carrying', is Latin's ordinary way of saying that a body has a part.

sentences.t:
Currebam: nec, ut ante, pedes retinebat harena,
sed summa tollebar humo. Mox alta per auras
evehor et data sum comes inculpata Minervae.
sentences.l: I was running: and the sand did not hold my feet back as before, but I was being lifted from the top of the ground. Soon I am carried high through the air, and was given to Minerva as a blameless companion.
sentences.i: I ran, and the sand no longer clogged my feet as it had: I was being lifted off the surface of the ground. Soon I am borne high through the air, and was given to Minerva for her blameless companion.
sentences.n: Summa humo is the same idiom as summa harena earlier — off the top of the ground, the point where running becomes flying. Evehor, a present, sits between two past tenses; the tense-shift lifts with her. Inculpata, 'unblamed', is the word she cares about most, and two lines on it stands against the diro crimine that won Nyctimene the place she lost.

sentences.t:
Quid tamen hoc prodest, si diro facta volucris
crimine Nyctimene nostro successit honori?
sentences.l: Yet what good is this, if Nyctimene, made a bird by a dreadful crime, has succeeded to my honour?
sentences.i: And what good is any of it, if Nyctimene, turned bird by a monstrous crime, has stepped into my place of honour?
sentences.n: Nostro is a poetic plural for meo — Latin verse uses 'our' for 'my' freely, and the reader has to hear the singular through it. Succedere takes the dative, 'to come in after' someone in a position. Diro crimine is ablative of cause, and the crime itself is named only in the next sentence: the crow holds it back to make you ask.

sentences.t:
An quae per totam res est notissima Lesbon,
non audita tibi est, patrium temerasse cubile
Nyctimenen?
sentences.l: Or has the thing best known through the whole of Lesbos not reached your ears — that Nyctimene defiled her father's bed?
sentences.i: Or have you not heard the story all Lesbos knows — that Nyctimene defiled her father's bed?
sentences.n: Lesbon and Nyctimenen both keep Greek accusative endings. The accusative and infinitive temerasse cubile stands in apposition to res, spelling out what the famous 'thing' is; temerasse is a syncopated perfect infinitive for temeravisse. Note whose account this is: the Latin puts the daughter in the accusative as the one who did it, and the crow, who has her own grievance, is glad to leave it there.

sentences.t:
avis illa quidem, sed conscia culpae
conspectum lucemque fugit tenebrisque pudorem
celat et a cunctis expellitur aethere toto.”
sentences.l: A bird she is, indeed, but knowing her own guilt she flees the sight of men and the daylight, and hides her shame in the darkness, and is driven out by all from the whole sky.
sentences.i: A bird she is, true enough; but conscious of her guilt she flees being looked at, and the light, and hides her shame in darkness, and every bird drives her out of the whole sky.
sentences.n: Conscia culpae takes the genitive and means sharing the knowledge of one's own guilt — the word is built for someone who cannot forget. Conspectum is the state of being seen, not the act of seeing. A cunctis means by all the other birds: the mobbing of an owl caught out in daylight is an observed fact, and Ovid turns it into a moral verdict.

sentences.t:
Talia dicenti “tibi” ait “revocamina” corvus
“sint precor ista malo: nos vanum spernimus omen.”
sentences.l: To her as she said such things the raven says: 'May those callings-back of yours be to your own hurt, I pray: we scorn an empty omen.'
sentences.i: To all this the raven answered: 'May your calling me back turn out badly for you, I pray. An empty omen is nothing to us.'
sentences.n: Talia dicenti is a dative depending on ait, 'to her as she said such things'; the same phrase returns at 665 to close Ocyrhoe's speech, and the echo pairs the two long warnings of this part. Revocamina is a rare noun, 'call-backs', more or less coined for the occasion. Sint … malo is an optative subjunctive with the same predicative dative that gave lingua fuit damno above, and nos is the poetic plural for 'I'.

sentences.t:
Nec coeptum dimittit iter, dominoque iacentem
cum iuvene Haemonio vidisse Coronida narrat.
sentences.l: Nor does he give up the journey he has begun, and he tells his master that he had seen Coronis lying with a Thessalian youth.
sentences.i: Nor did he drop the journey he had begun: he told his master he had seen Coronis lying with a young Thessalian.
sentences.n: Coronida is a Greek accusative. Vidisse is an accusative and infinitive after narrat, and it is worth noticing what the raven now claims: earlier the bird only sensit, sensed, the adultery; in the telling it has become something he saw. Iacentem cum is the plain, unliterary phrase for it, and Ovid does not decorate it.

sentences.t:
Laurea delapsa est audito crimine amanti,
et pariter vultusque deo plectrumque colorque
excidit.
sentences.l: The laurel slipped from the lover as the charge was heard, and together the god's face and plectrum and colour fell away.
sentences.i: At the charge the laurel slipped from the lover's head, and all at once his expression, his plectrum and his colour dropped from the god.
sentences.n: Audito crimine is an ablative absolute again, and amanti a dative of separation, 'from the lover' — Ovid calls him the lover here and not the god, which is the point of the line. One singular verb, excidit, serves three subjects at once, and it is literally true only of the plectrum: the face and the colour fall away in a different sense, and the yoking of the three is the shock.

sentences.t:
Utque animus tumida fervebat ab ira,
arma adsueta rapit flexumque a cornibus arcum
tendit et illa suo totiens cum pectore iuncta
indevitato traiecit pectora telo.
sentences.l: And as his heart boiled with swollen anger, he snatches up his familiar weapons and bends the bow curved back from its horns, and with a shaft there was no dodging he shot through that breast which had so often been joined to his own.
sentences.i: And as his heart boiled up with swelling rage, he caught up the weapons he knew so well, drew the bow bent back from its horn-tips, and with an arrow no one escapes pierced the breast that had lain against his own so many times.
sentences.n: Adsueta keeps the edition's ad- spelling and means the weapons that are habitual to him: the bow is his own attribute, which is what makes this a domestic murder rather than an execution. Illa … pectora … iuncta is split across a line and a half, the adjective waiting the whole time for its noun, and the delay is the cruelty. Magnus prints rapit, 'snatches'; some editions print capit, 'takes', which lets a good deal of the violence out of the gesture.

sentences.t:
Icta dedit gemitum, tractoque a corpore ferro
candida puniceo perfudit membra cruore,
sentences.l: Struck, she gave a groan, and when the iron had been drawn from her body she drenched her white limbs with crimson blood,
sentences.n: Icta, a single participle, carries the whole blow: Latin can do in one word what English needs a clause for. Tracto a corpore ferro is another ablative absolute. Candida and puniceo are set against each other across the line, white against red — the colour opposition that has run through this part since the raven's feathers, and it lands here on a body.

sentences.t:
et dixit: “Potui poenas tibi, Phoebe, dedisse,
sed peperisse prius: duo nunc moriemur in una.”
sentences.l: and said: 'I might have paid you the penalty, Phoebus — but borne my child first: now two of us will die in one.'
sentences.i: and said: 'I could have paid you my penalty, Phoebus — but let me bear the child first. Now two of us die in one.'
sentences.n: Potui with the perfect infinitives dedisse and peperisse expresses a possibility that is now closed off: it could have gone the other way, and it did not. She does not deny the charge. Duo … in una counts the unborn child as the second of the two and leaves 'in one what' unsaid — in one woman, in one body, in one death. These are the only words she is given.

sentences.t:
Hactenus, et pariter vitam cum sanguine fudit.
Corpus inane animae frigus letale secutum est.
sentences.l: So far, and at once she poured out her life together with her blood. A deadly chill followed the body once emptied of its soul.
sentences.i: So far and no further: she poured out her life with her blood, and a deadly chill came over the body the soul had left.
sentences.n: Hactenus stands alone with no verb — 'so far [she spoke]' — so the grammar breaks off exactly where the speech does. Fudit is the same verb used of the blood a line earlier, which makes life and blood one substance running out. Inane animae, an adjective with a genitive of separation, is a Greek-flavoured construction rather than an ordinary Latin one.
sentences.mark: Her one speech ends mid-breath, and Ovid gives the sentence no verb.

sentences.t:
Paenitet heu sero poenae crudelis amantem,
seque, quod audierit, quod sic exarserit, odit;
sentences.l: Too late, alas, the lover repents of his cruel punishment, and hates himself for having listened, for having blazed up so;
sentences.n: Paenitet is impersonal and takes the person in the accusative (amantem) and the thing in the genitive (poenae): 'it repents the lover of the punishment'. Quod with the subjunctive audierit gives the reason as his own thought, not the poet's. And Ovid still will not call him Apollo — he is 'the lover' at the moment when the title costs most.

sentences.t:
odit avem, per quam crimen causamque dolendi
scire coactus erat, nec non arcumque manumque
odit,
sentences.l: he hates the bird through which he had been forced to know the charge and the cause of his grieving, and no less does he hate the bow and the hand,
sentences.i: he hates the bird that forced him to learn the charge and the reason for his grief; and no less he hates the bow, and the hand,
sentences.n: Odit falls three times in three lines, each time at the head or the tail of its clause, so the hatred can be watched spreading outward: himself, then the bird, then his own hand. Nec non is litotes, a double negative that comes out stronger than a plain 'also'. Causam dolendi puts the gerund in the genitive, 'the cause of grieving'.

sentences.t:
cumque manu temeraria tela sagittas
conlapsamque fovet seraque ope vincere fata
nititur et medicas exercet inaniter artes.
sentences.l: and along with the hand the reckless weapons, the arrows; and he cherishes her where she has fallen, and strives with help come too late to overcome the fates, and plies his healing arts to no purpose.
sentences.i: and along with his hand the reckless weapons, the arrows. He gathers her fallen body to him, strives with help that comes too late to overcome the fates, and works his healing arts for nothing.
sentences.n: Temeraria tela sagittas is asyndeton — no 'and' between them, the second noun simply naming the first more exactly, as a man might correct himself. Fovet is what one does to keep a body warm. Medicas artes is the sting: this is the god of healing, and inaniter picks up the tempora inania that the sea-god wasted on his coaxing.

sentences.t:
Quae postquam frustra temptata, rogumque parari
vidit et arsuros supremis ignibus artus,
sentences.l: And when these had been tried in vain, and he saw the pyre being made ready and the limbs that would burn in the last fires,
sentences.n: Quae opening the sentence is the connecting relative once more, 'and these things'. Temptata has lost its auxiliary verb, an ellipsis that verse permits everywhere. Arsuros is a future participle, the limbs 'about to burn'; suprema, the 'last things', is the ordinary Latin word for funeral rites, so the fire is named by what it is for.

sentences.t:
tum vero gemitus (neque enim caelestia tingi
ora licet lacrimis) alto de corde petitos
edidit,
sentences.l: then indeed he let out groans fetched from deep in his heart — for heavenly faces may not be wetted with tears —
sentences.i: then he let out groans drawn up from the bottom of his heart, since a god's face is not permitted to be wet with tears;
sentences.n: The parenthesis explains the groans: he would weep if he could, and divine law does not allow it, so the grief has to leave him by another route. Licet takes an accusative and infinitive, caelestia ora tingi. Gemitus and its participle petitos stand on either side of the bracket, so the reader has to hold the phrase open across the interruption — the sentence is made to strain, like the god.

sentences.t:
haud aliter quam cum spectante iuvenca
lactentis vituli, dextra libratus ab aure
tempora discussit claro cava malleus ictu.
sentences.l: not otherwise than when, the heifer looking on, the mallet, swung back from beside the right ear, has shattered the hollow temples of a suckling calf with a ringing blow.
sentences.i: just as when, while the mother cow looks on, the mallet, swung back past the right ear, smashes in the hollow temples of a suckling calf with one bright, ringing blow.
sentences.n: Spectante iuvenca is an ablative absolute, and it is the whole force of the simile: the parent who can only watch. Dextra ab aure is where the slaughterer's swing starts, cava tempora the hollow at the temple where the blow is aimed, and claro is a description of the sound. The perfect discussit is gnomic — it states what happens every time, not what happened once.

sentences.t:
Ut tamen ingratos in pectora fudit odores
et dedit amplexus iniustaque iusta peregit,
sentences.l: Yet when he had poured unwelcome perfumes upon her breast, and given her his embraces, and carried out the unjust due rites,
sentences.i: Still, when he had poured the perfumes she could not thank him for over her breast, and embraced her, and performed the funeral dues that were undue,
sentences.n: Ingratos means both unwelcomed and unthanked, and neither sense works without the other: she cannot receive them and cannot acknowledge them. Iusta in the neuter plural is the technical word for funeral rites, 'the things owed'. Iniusta iusta sets the two senses of what is due against each other in one breath — an untranslatable pun, and it is meant to hurt.

sentences.l: Phoebus did not bear that his own seed should sink into those same ashes, but tore his son from the flames and from the mother's womb, and carried him into the cave of double-formed Chiron;
sentences.i: Phoebus would not have his own seed sink into the same ashes: he tore his son out of the flames and out of the mother's womb, and carried him to the cave of two-formed Chiron;
sentences.n: Non tulit takes an accusative and infinitive, 'he did not endure that …'. Sua semina is a poetic plural for his seed. Tulit does duty twice in three lines, once meaning to endure and once to carry, and the repetition is not carelessness. Geminus of Chiron — half man, half horse — is the same adjective used of Cecrops earlier in the crow's tale.

sentences.t:
sperantemque sibi non falsae praemia linguae
inter aves albas vetuit consistere corvum.
sentences.l: and the raven, hoping for himself the reward of a tongue that had not lied, he forbade to take his place among the white birds.
sentences.i: and the raven, who was expecting a reward for a tongue that had told no lie, he forbade to stand among the white birds.
sentences.n: Non falsae linguae is litotes, 'a tongue not false' — the understatement makes the injustice colder than an outright 'truthful' would. Consistere is to take up one's standing place, of a bird settling with a flock. This is where the colour promised back at the start finally arrives: the tale of why white became white's opposite is closed, and the crow's argument that honesty does harm is proved.

sentences.t:
Semifer interea divinae stirpis alumno
laetus erat mixtoque oneri gaudebat honore.
sentences.l: Meanwhile the half-beast was glad of his nursling of divine stock, and took joy in the honour mixed into the burden.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the half-beast rejoiced in his nursling of divine blood, and in the honour that came mixed with the charge.
sentences.n: Semifer, 'half wild animal', is all the name Chiron gets here, and the Latin lets the word carry the whole picture. Alumno is an ablative of cause with laetus. Mixto … honore is an ablative wrapped right round the dative oneri, so that fostering becomes a single figure — an honour stirred into a burden — which the reader has to assemble from the endings.

sentences.t:
Ecce venit rutilis umeros protecta capillis
filia Centauri, quam quondam nympha Chariclo
fluminis in rapidi ripis enixa vocavit
Ocyroen.
sentences.l: Behold, the Centaur's daughter comes, covered as to her shoulders with glowing red hair, whom once the nymph Chariclo, having borne her on the banks of a rushing river, called Ocyrhoe.
sentences.i: Look — the Centaur's daughter comes, her shoulders covered with red-gold hair: the nymph Chariclo bore her on the banks of a rushing river, and named her Ocyrhoe.
sentences.n: Umeros protecta is the Greek accusative of respect after a passive participle — covered, and the accusative says as to what. Latin borrowed the construction from Greek and Ovid uses it constantly for clothing, veiling and wounds. Ocyroen keeps its Greek accusative, and the name is held back to the head of the next line, where it arrives just after the swift river it was taken from.

sentences.t:
Non haec artes contenta paternas
edidicisse fuit: fatorum arcana canebat.
sentences.l: She was not content to have learned her father's arts right through: she sang the secrets of the fates.
sentences.i: She was not content with having learned her father's arts by heart: she sang the secrets of the fates.
sentences.n: Contenta takes a perfect infinitive, edidicisse, whose prefix means learning a thing right through to the end. Canere is the technical verb for prophesying: a seer does not state, a seer sings, and the same word covers poetry, which is not an accident in a poem. The Latin names her father's arts only as paternae — Chiron's are the healing arts — and says she has gone past them to what the fates keep hidden.

sentences.t:
Ergo ubi vaticinos concepit mente furores
incaluitque deo, quem clausum pectore habebat,
adspicit infantem “toto” que “salutifer orbi
cresce puer” dixit:
sentences.l: So when she had conceived prophetic frenzies in her mind and grew hot with the god she kept shut in her breast, she looks on the infant and said: 'Grow, boy, health-bringer to the whole world:'
sentences.i: So when she had taken the prophetic frenzy into her mind and caught fire from the god she kept shut inside her breast, she looked at the baby and said: 'Grow, child, healer of the whole world:'
sentences.n: Incaluit deo — 'grew hot with the god' — is the same verb used of the sea-god's lust in the crow's story: possession and desire are described by Ovid with one vocabulary of heat. Salutifer is a compound of the kind Latin builds freely and English does not: health-bringing. Ovid's own -que breaks into the quotation after its first word, and the vocative puer is held to the very end, so 'health-bringer to the whole world' arrives before the reader learns who is being addressed.

sentences.l: to you mortal bodies will often owe themselves; it will be right for you to give back souls once taken away;
sentences.i: mortal bodies will often owe themselves to you; it will be permitted to you to give back souls that have been taken away;
sentences.n: Se debebunt, 'will owe themselves', says more than 'will owe their lives': men will be in his debt for their own existence. Fas is what divine law permits, as against ius, which is human law — and the word is chosen with care, because the next sentence is about that permission being withdrawn. Ademptas, 'taken away', is the standard word for a life cut short.

sentences.t:
idque semel dis indignantibus ausus
posse dare hoc iterum flamma prohibebere avita
eque deo corpus fies exsangue, deusque,
qui modo corpus eras, et bis tua fata novabis.
sentences.l: and having once dared it, to the gods' indignation, you will be barred by your grandfather's fire from being able to give it a second time; and from a god you will become a bloodless body, and a god again, you who a moment before were a body — and twice you will make your own destiny new.
sentences.i: and having dared it once, with the gods indignant, you will be stopped by your grandfather's flame from ever giving it again: from a god you will become a bloodless corpse, and then a god again, you who a moment before were a corpse — twice over you will make your fate new.
sentences.n: Dis indignantibus is an ablative absolute. Flamma avita, 'the ancestral flame', is the lightning of Jupiter, who is Apollo's father and so the child's grandfather — the Latin names neither of them and expects the family tree to be supplied. Prohibebere is the alternative second-person passive ending in -re for -ris, common in verse. The word order e deo corpus … deus qui corpus eras crosses over itself, so the sentence performs the double reversal it predicts.

sentences.t:
Tu quoque, care pater, nunc inmortalis et aevis
omnibus ut maneas nascendi lege creatus,
posse mori cupies, tum cum cruciabere dirae
sanguine serpentis per saucia membra recepto;
sentences.l: You too, dear father, now immortal and made by the law of your birth to remain through every age, will long to be able to die, in the hour when you are tortured by the blood of a dreadful serpent taken in through your wounded limbs;
sentences.i: You too, dear father, immortal now, made by the terms of your birth to last through every age, will long for the power to die, in the hour when the blood of a dreadful serpent, taken in through your torn limbs, tortures you;
sentences.n: Quoque here is the plain adverb, 'you as well' — but be careful with the word, because it is just as often quo-que, 'and with which', and the two are spelled identically. Nascendi lege creatus makes his immortality a condition of birth rather than a reward: he cannot resign it. Sanguine … recepto is not an ablative absolute but the ablative of means with cruciabere — the serpent's blood itself does the torturing, taken in through the wounded limbs.

sentences.t:
teque ex aeterno patientem numina mortis
efficient, triplicesque deae tua fila resolvent.”
sentences.l: and the divine powers will make you, from being eternal, able to suffer death, and the threefold goddesses will unloose your threads.
sentences.i: and the gods will make you, who were eternal, able to suffer death; and the three goddesses will loose your threads.
sentences.n: Ex aeterno uses the adjective as a noun for the state he is leaving — 'out of being eternal'. Patientem mortis takes the genitive and means capable of undergoing death, not merely willing to. The triplices deae are the three Fates, who spin, measure and cut the thread of every life, so fila, 'threads', is not a metaphor here but the thing itself.

sentences.t:
Restabat fatis aliquid. Suspirat ab imis
pectoribus, lacrimaeque genis labuntur obortae,
sentences.l: Something still remained for the fates. She sighs from the bottom of her breast, and tears well up and slip down her cheeks,
sentences.i: There was still something of the fates left to say. She sighs from the depths of her breast, and tears rise and slide down her cheeks,
sentences.n: Fatis is a dative: something was still left for the fates — still owing, still to be disclosed — and four words turn the scene, because we are about to be told that we will not hear it. Pectoribus is a poetic plural for one breast. Obortae, 'having risen up', is used of tears that come unbidden, which is the difference between weeping and being wept out of.

sentences.t:
atque ita “praevertunt” inquit “me fata, vetorque
plura loqui, vocisque meae praecluditur usus.
sentences.l: and so she says: 'The fates outrun me, and I am forbidden to say more, and the use of my voice is being shut off.'
sentences.i: and so she said: 'The fates are outrunning me. I am forbidden to speak further, and the use of my voice is being closed off.'
sentences.n: Praevertere is to get in front of, to forestall — the fates arrive before her words can reach them. Vetor with an infinitive is a personal passive, where English prefers the impersonal 'it is forbidden'. Praecludere is used of blocking a road or damming a channel, so the voice is being stopped like water.

sentences.t:
Non fuerant artes tanti, quae numinis iram
contraxere mihi; mallem nescisse futura.
sentences.l: They had not been worth so much, these arts which drew a god's anger down upon me; I would rather not have known the future.
sentences.i: They were not worth it, these arts that have drawn a god's anger down on me. I would rather never have known what was coming.
sentences.n: Tanti is a genitive of value, 'worth so much'. Contraxere is contraxerunt — the third-plural perfect in -ere is everywhere in this poem and means exactly what the -erunt form means; verse prefers it for its shorter ending. Mallem with the perfect infinitive nescisse is a wish for something that can no longer be arranged.

sentences.t:
Iam mihi subduci facies humana videtur,
iam cibus herba placet, iam latis currere campis
impetus est: in equam cognataque corpora vertor.
Tota tamen quare? pater est mihi nempe biformis.”
sentences.l: Already my human face seems to be taken from me, already grass pleases me for food, already the urge is on me to run over the wide fields: I am being turned into a mare, into a body of my own kin. Yet why all of me? My father, after all, is two-formed.
sentences.i: Already my human face seems to be slipping away from me; already grass is what I want to eat; already the urge is on me to run the wide fields. I am turning into a mare, into a body of my own blood. Yet why the whole of me? My father, after all, is two-formed.
sentences.n: Three iam's in two lines, each marking a further stage — the change is happening inside the speech that reports it, which is why she has to keep starting again. Cognata corpora, 'kindred body', is literally true: her father is half horse. And the last thing she says is a joke, and a question, and nobody answers it.

sentences.t:
Talia dicenti pars est extrema querellae
intellecta parum, confusaque verba fuerunt.
sentences.l: To her as she said such things, the last part of the complaint was too little understood, and the words were confused.
sentences.i: As she said such things, the last part of her lament was barely understood: the words came out blurred.
sentences.n: Talia dicenti is the same dative Ovid used at 596, where the raven brushed the crow's warning aside; here no verb of speaking governs it, so it hangs as the dative of the person concerned. The echo pairs the two long speeches of this part — one answered and dismissed, one cut off mid-sentence. Parum means too little, not merely little, and querella covers both a lament and a formal complaint; the tale has grounds for either.

sentences.t:
Mox nec verba quidem nec equae sonus ille videtur,
sed simulantis equam, parvoque in tempore certos
edidit hinnitus et bracchia movit in herbas.
sentences.l: Soon that sound seems neither words nor a mare's, but one imitating a mare's; and in a little while she gave out unmistakable whinnies, and moved her arms down into the grass.
sentences.i: Soon that sound seems to be neither words nor a mare's voice, but the voice of someone imitating a mare; and in a little while she was giving out unmistakable whinnies and moving her arms down into the grass.
sentences.n: Two genitives hang on sonus: the sound of a mare, then the sound of someone doing an imitation of a mare — and the second is the more unnerving of the two, because it still has a person in it. Certos means unmistakable, the moment the imitation stops being one. And they are still arms in the Latin when they come down to the grass; Ovid holds the word one line longer than the body deserves.

sentences.t:
Tum digiti coeunt et quinos adligat ungues
perpetuo cornu levis ungula, crescit et oris
et colli spatium, longae pars maxima pallae
cauda fit,
sentences.l: Then the fingers close together, and a smooth hoof binds the five nails in unbroken horn; the reach of her mouth and of her neck grows; the greatest part of her long robe becomes a tail,
sentences.i: Then her fingers close together, and a smooth hoof binds all five nails in a single unbroken horn; her mouth and neck stretch out; the greater part of her long robe becomes a tail,
sentences.n: Quinos is the distributive numeral, 'five apiece' — Ovid is counting both hands at once without saying so. Perpetuo cornu, 'with continuous horn', is the hoof described as what it replaces: one nail where there were five. Spatium oris et colli, the 'extent' of mouth and neck, is a cold, measuring word for a muzzle lengthening. Clothing turning into body is the standard hinge of a metamorphosis in this poem.

sentences.t:
utque vagi crines per colla iacebant,
in dextras abiere iubas: pariterque novata est
et vox et facies nomen quoque monstra dedere.
sentences.l: and as her loose hair lay along her neck, it passed off into a mane on the right; and alike were made new both her voice and her face — the marvels gave her a name too.
sentences.i: and as her loose hair lay along her neck, it went over into a mane falling to the right; her voice and her face were made new together — and the marvels gave her a new name as well.
sentences.n: In dextras iubas is an observed detail: a horse's mane falls to the right side. Abiere and dedere are both third-plural perfects in -ere, for abierunt and dederunt. Monstra, 'portents, wonders', is the subject of the last verb, so it is the transformation itself that does the naming — and the name is never given. The tale is left standing on the word for marvels.
